name: Aisha Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or any government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mondays and Thursdays I'm in lectures from nine, mostly programming basics and maths that I'm already behind on. I live at home with my mum, who drives a city bus, so I take the 7:10 to campus. Tuesday and Saturday evenings I stack shelves at a supermarket until ten. By Sunday I'm trying to catch up on labs, and honestly I'm tired already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's what I expected. The tech companies were always going to oversell it, and I'm not surprised the magic never showed up. At my supermarket they keep promising self-checkouts will fix everything and then someone has to stand next to them anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my degree stays a normal degree, which is a relief, but it doesn't solve anything. I still owe loan money, and the graduate jobs were already thin before AI came along. My course mates talk like there's a job waiting at the end, and I'm not so sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going exactly as I am. Keep the two shifts, keep my head down in labs, and try to pass first year without failing the maths module. I'd also ask my mum if I can stay at home through the whole degree, because that's what keeps me afloat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, mostly. It's the old worries, money and grades, rather than a new one. I feel a bit tired of people making a drama about every new thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said graduate jobs were thin already. What makes you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin finished business two years ago and spent eight months sending applications. He ended up at a call centre. Nobody told him it would be like that, and I'm in a harder subject but with average grades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And which bill gets squeezed first if shifts get cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My phone contract, then my bus pass top-up. I'd never touch the money I give my mum for food, because she's already stretching her pay to cover the gas bill.

say: I'm not surprised **AI is hype**, because companies always oversell things.
My supermarket's self-checkouts still need a person standing next to them.
think: My degree stays ordinary, but the **graduate jobs** were thin before AI arrived.
I still carry **loan debt** and a fear that average grades won't be enough.
do: **Keep** both supermarket shifts and keep passing labs.
Ask my mum to let me **stay at home** for the whole degree.
feel: Tired and **uneasy** about money, but not afraid of AI itself.
S0.quote: I still owe loan money, and the graduate jobs were already thin before AI came along.
fieldNote: Her worry here is **money** and grades, not AI; she is already carrying the pressure.
Distrusts **tech company** promises and links it to what she sees at work.
**Thin savings** and few local jobs keep the mood from being calm.

steps.text: Keep both supermarket shifts through first year
Stay in mum's house for the whole degree
Cut the phone contract before touching food money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what we were warned about, and it's going to hit people like me first. Writing, checking, coding, those are the things my course teaches. I'd say the companies are taking the benefit and ordinary people carry the risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm scared that entry-level coding jobs are the first ones to go. Why would a firm hire a junior when software does the checking? My lecturer said the junior roles are already shrinking, and I'm in the average group, not the top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying, because I can't see another option, and I'd look into the students' union and any group fighting for rules about AI in hiring. I'd probably try to get a part-time job that's actually technical, even office IT help, so I have something on the CV. I still wouldn't use the AI tools myself, though. I don't trust them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. I feel like the ground is moving and everyone else has a better pair of shoes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't use the AI tools. Doesn't that put you behind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, yes. But I'd rather learn the actual maths underneath than be someone who types a question and pastes an answer. If the job needs the tool, I can learn it in a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the junior jobs disappear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firms that cut them to save money, and the government that lets them. Nobody voted for it, and there should be rules that say you must train young people.

say: The **companies** are keeping the gains while ordinary people take the risk.
The **junior coding jobs** are the first ones that software will take.
think: I'm in the **average** group, so a shrinking graduate pool lands on me.
I don't trust AI tools, but I know **refusing** may hold me back.
do: Join the **students' union** and push for rules on AI in hiring.
Look for a part-time **IT help** job to put on my CV.
feel: **Heavy** and a little angry, as if everyone else started with better shoes.
S1.quote: Why would a firm hire a junior when software does the checking?
fieldNote: **Anger** is aimed at firms and government, in line with her left-leaning, pro-union views.
**Refuses** AI tools out of distrust but accepts she could learn them fast if the job needed it.
Expects her own **entry route** route to shrink, but still believes she has some control.

steps.text: Join the students' union and push for hiring rules
Apply for part-time IT help desk jobs on campus
Keep studying maths properly instead of copying answers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a disaster in waiting, and governments should be shouting about it, not sleeping through it. Two years is nothing. I'd be posting in student groups that we need laws now, and that firms should be taxed so ordinary people get some of what AI earns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my degree might be worthless before I finish it. I'm in first year, I'll be done in 2029, and by then the thinking jobs I'm studying for are gone. My mum's bus job would last longer than my career, which is a strange thing to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd stay at home and save every pound I can, because I'd have no idea what comes next. I'd go to every protest and union meeting I could find, and I'd probably switch to something hands-on, maybe an apprenticeship in electrical work, if my university lets me leave without a huge bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Terrified, to be honest. I'd not be sleeping properly. I'd keep thinking about the loan and nothing to pay it with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your mum's bus job. What do you think happens to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots for hands-on work come about three years after, so around 2031. That gives her some years, but buses already have driverless trials, and she knows it. We haven't talked about it. I don't want to scare her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it take for you to leave the degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A clear sign the job market is closing, like the first big firms announcing they've stopped hiring graduates. Then I'd go straight to an apprenticeship, because at least that's paid.

say: **Two years** is nothing, and governments are sleeping through it.
Firms should be **taxed** so ordinary people share in what AI earns.
think: My degree could be **worthless** before I finish in 2029.
My mum's **bus job** might outlast my career, which is a strange thing.
do: **Save** every spare pound while staying at my mum's house.
Switch to an **electrical apprenticeship** if the university lets me leave cheaply.
feel: **Terrified**, with poor sleep and a loan I might never repay.
S2.quote: My mum's bus job would last longer than my career, which is a strange thing to say.
fieldNote: Expects the **whole career** she is studying for to vanish, with debt already in place.
Thinks about her **mother's** job's job but has avoided the conversation.
Has a **concrete fallback**: an apprenticeship if she can leave the degree cheaply.

steps.text: Save every spare pound and stay at home
Go to union meetings and a protest every month
Ask the university about leaving for an electrical apprenticeship
Write to my MP about taxing AI profits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives the government time to act if it wants to, so no excuses. We'd need retraining paid for properly and a rule about firms having to give young people jobs. I'd say it in the union and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's still frightening, but it feels like I'd have a fair fight. By 2031 I'll have graduated, and I'd be looking for a job at the exact moment AI can do the thinking work. It's the worst timing for me. Hands-on work would follow in 2034, which is why I'd think about a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the first two years and see what's happening in the job market. Meanwhile I'd start learning something physical on the side, like wiring with my uncle who's an electrician. I'd also save at least a hundred a month, even if it means dropping the nights out I barely have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but not hopeless. Five years is long enough to build a plan, and I like having a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd start with wiring. Why wiring rather than another computing area?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people will always need a house wired, and a robot with arms only arrives around 2034. It buys me some years. My uncle says there's more work than electricians at the moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your mum say about you leaving computing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be relieved, I think. She never understood why I wanted to sit in front of a screen. But she'd worry about me wasting the loan.

say: Five years means the **government** has no excuse not to act.
We need **paid retraining** and rules that make firms hire young people.
think: I'd graduate right when AI does the **thinking work**, the worst timing.
Hands-on jobs last until about **2034**, so a trade buys me years.
do: Learn **wiring** with my uncle at weekends over the next two years.
**Save** at least a hundred a month, even by dropping nights out.
feel: **Nervous** but not hopeless, since five years is long enough for a plan.
S3.quote: By 2031 I'll have graduated, and I'd be looking for a job at the exact moment AI can do the thinking work.
fieldNote: **Time** lets her plan, and the plan is a trade, which fits her cautious, practical side.
Still puts the **responsibility** responsibility on government and firms rather than herself.
Her **uncle** is a real route, so her worry is shaped by a concrete option.

steps.text: Learn basic wiring with my uncle at weekends
Save a hundred a month from shop wages
Review the job market again at the end of second year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough to get ready, and I'd urge everyone to stop treating this like a movie. There's time to change laws, build new training and protect people who lose out. I'd also tell people to join a union now, not later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels survivable. I'd be 28 and mid-career by 2036, so I'd have time to land a job, pay off a chunk of my loan and see how things go. It's not great, but it's not 2028. I'd even finish my degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish, get a first job, and in the meantime learn a bit about how the AI tools work, even though I hate that. If I'm in the industry, I should understand what is replacing the industry. I'd also put money in a pension from my first paycheck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the other ones. There's still a worry, but I can see a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you hate learning the AI tools. What changed your mind here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The time. With two years I'd have no choice but to run. With ten, I can learn them slowly and still keep my own way of thinking. I just don't want to be the person who can't explain the code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell yourself at 18 about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stop treating every setback as the end. Finish the degree, keep the supermarket job until you have a better one, and look after your mum.

say: A **decade** is enough to build training and protect people who lose out.
I'd tell everyone to join a **union** now, not later.
think: By 2036 I'd be 28 with a **job** and some loan paid off, so it's survivable.
I should understand the **AI tools** that might replace my field.
do: **Finish** the degree and aim for a first graduate job.
Learn the AI tools **slowly** alongside my own coding practice.
feel: **Calmer** than in the faster pictures, and I can see a path.
S4.quote: With two years I'd have no choice but to run. With ten, I can learn them slowly and still keep my own way of thinking.
fieldNote: **Time** moves her from alarm to unease, but loan debt keeps some worry in place.
Willing to touch **AI tools** AI tools only when she is not forced to, which fits her resistant profile.
Looks after her **mother** in her plans, which gives her a clear sense of stakes.

steps.text: Finish the degree and apply for graduate jobs in year three
Learn how AI coding tools work, one evening a week
Start a pension from the first graduate paycheck

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because two years is not enough to do anything. What would help is the government paying for retraining and making firms keep hiring young people. And my university should be honest about whether my course will still lead somewhere, instead of just taking the fees.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my mum. I'm not afraid of the machines. I'm afraid that a few companies will keep the money and people like my mum will get told to adapt. She's the reason I'm not panicking, and she's the one I'm most worried about if robots get to the buses. I'd like her to be safe before I'm comfortable.

headlineQuote: I'm not afraid of the machines. I'm afraid that a few companies will keep the money and people like my mum will get told to adapt.
portrait: Aisha is an 18-year-old **computing** student living at her mum's house, working two supermarket shifts and distrusting AI tools.
She leans left, blames **firms and governments** rather than the technology, and is drawn to unions and regulation.
Her thin savings and average grades make her anxious in even the mild pictures, and **alarmed** if AGI arrives by 2028.
She would rather learn the maths than the tools, and keeps an **electrical apprenticeship** as her fallback.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries her most, since two years is too short to plan.
whatWouldHelp: Government-paid **retraining** and a rule that firms keep hiring young people.
Her university being **honest** about what her course leads to.
